title: Networking hardening playbook — VPC & on-prem Terraform patterns
content:
Purpose
This is a working playbook for hardening networking in Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). Focus is on repeatable Terraform module patterns, staged firewall/ingress promotion, per-tenant NAT segmentation, private DNS design (split-horizon + forwarders), and a pragmatic upgrade/rollback plan for network changes that can affect live inference traffic.

Scope and constraints
- Target environments: customer VPCs (AWS/GCP/Azure patterns) and on-prem racks with virtual networking (OVN/MetalLB/Cilium).
- This doc assumes a two-plane model: control-plane traffic (management/control plane agents, telemetry) vs data-plane (inference traffic, model downloads).
- Goal: zero or minimal customer-facing downtime during network changes. Changes that require short maintenance windows must be signaled and instrumented.

High-level goals
- Least-privilege firewall rules by role: management, admin, service, metadata, prometheus/scrape.
- Isolate tenant egress via per-tenant NAT (SNAT pools) or egress proxies.
- Preserve DNS privacy: use split-horizon for internal names, conditional forwarders to customer DNS for on-prem resolvability.
- Make Terraform modules composable and idempotent; keep network state in remote state backend with locks.

Design patterns and Terraform notes
1) Module composition pattern (recommended)
- network-core: subnets, route tables, k8s node SGs/NSGs
- dns: private hosted zones, conditional forwarders, resolver endpoints
- nat: nat-gateway module with allocation pools, route table attachments
- firewall: security group / firewalls module with policy sets (env, role)
- ingress: lb + private ingress controller configuration (health checks, source ranges)

Notes:
- Prefer smaller modules that expose clear inputs (subnet ids, tag maps) and return outputs for downstream modules.
- Avoid cross-module resource creation (e.g., have network-core create route tables; nat module only creates gateways and returns IDs to be used by network-core).

2) Firewall rule pattern: staged promotion
- Stages: 'plan' -> 'staged' -> 'apply-live' -> 'audit'.
- In Terraform flow:
  a) Create a "staged" security_group/resource with name prefix "staged/2024-08-<ticket>" that references the same targets as existing production SGs via tags.
  b) Run integration smoke tests (see test checklist) while only traffic from canary CIDRs allowed.
  c) When smoke passes, swap references at higher level: update route/attachment to point to staged SG or gradually loosen prod rule.
  d) Keep staged object for 72 hours for audit; then remove.

Example simplified HCL (pattern, not copy-paste):
resource "aws_security_group" "svc_staged" {
  name        = "staged-${var.ticket}-svc"
  description = "Staged rules for canary promotion"
  vpc_id      = var.vpc_id
  ingress = [
    { from_port = 443, to_port = 443, protocol = "tcp", cidr_blocks = var.canary_cidrs }
  ]
  tags = merge(var.common_tags, {"promote-ticket" = var.ticket, "staged" = "true"})
}

3) Per-tenant NAT segmentation
- Motivation: restrict cross-tenant egress, audit per-tenant flows, support customer-requested egress IP allowlists.
- Approaches:
  a) Dedicated NAT Gateway per tenant/az (costly but simplest isolation)
  b) Shared NAT + source-based IP masquerade with NAT pools (cheaper, needs mapping table)
  c) Egress proxy (squid/tproxy/sidecar) for fine-grained controls and SNI inspection (adds latency)

Recommendations:
- For enterprise customers requiring IP allowlists, prefer dedicated NAT per tenant (or per-tenant egress pools) and provide a Terraform input map of tenant_id -> nat_pool_ids.
- Provide a fallback path: when a tenant-level NAT is unavailable, fall back to a less-restrictive shared NAT with logging and an alert.

4) Private DNS: split-horizon + conditional forwarders
- Use private hosted zones for internal service names (e.g., *.internal.redwood) and conditional forwarders to customer DNS for on-prem-resolvable names.
- For cloud: use resolver endpoints (Route 53 Resolver / Cloud DNS) with conditional forwarder rules. For on-prem: deploy lightweight forwarders (dnsmasq) in jump subnets with same ACLs.
- Key settings:
  - TTLs: keep internal host TTLs low (60s) during rollout, then raise to 300s when stable.
  - Health-checks for DNS entries tied to LB health to avoid stale resolution.

5) Ingress topology (private LB patterns)
- Prefer regional/internal load balancers with health checks and strict backend security groups that only accept from LB.
- For on-prem, use MetalLB + private VIPs and advertise via BGP (or static route) into customer network.
- Ensure health check ACLs and source ranges are explicit; do not have broad 0.0.0.0/0 open unless explicitly for internet-facing endpoints.

Upgrade plan for network changes (safe path)
- Pre-steps: create a dedicated Terraform plan workspace with remote state snapshot. Open a change-request ticket with owner and risk level.
- Phase A: dry-run and unit tests (terraform plan + static checks)
- Phase B: apply to non-prod environment and run end-to-end smoke (canary model load, tokenized inference calls, trace latency). Observe metrics for minimum 2 business cycles.
- Phase C: staged rollout to production using traffic shaping (canary CIDRs or subset of nodes). Keep rate limits low. Monitor errors, latency, and logs.
- Phase D: promote staged to global after 24–72h of stable metrics.

Rollback plan
- Preserve last-known-good state as a Terraform workspace snapshot. For single-rule revocations, revert the staged change by re-applying previous SG/rule state.
- For route changes: have pre-created rollback-route tables and weighted route policies that can be toggled quickly.
- For NAT/egress IP changes: maintain previous NAT allocation in a 'warm' state for 30 minutes so DB connections and long-lived sessions can drain before full switch.

Test checklist (smoke and pre-promote)
- DNS resolution: dig against resolver endpoints for internal names and conditional forwarders.
- Ingress health: curl LB VIP from allowed CIDR and verify 200 + headers contain expected trace IDs.
- Egress mapping: from tenant namespace, curl httpbin.org/ip to confirm SNAT address matches expected pool.
- Firewall enforcement: attempt denied connection from disallowed CIDR and confirm connection reset/timeout.
- Observability: confirm spans propagate through tracing and logs show new rule annotations.

Runbook commands and diagnostics (examples)
- Check SGs / firewall rules (AWS CLI): aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC_ID}
- Check route tables: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids ${RT_ID}
- Validate DNS forwarding: dig @${RESOLVER_IP} internal.service.internal +short
- Check NAT mappings (cloud): aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC_ID}

Monitoring and alerting to add before change
- Egress IP drift alert: when observed egress IPs for a tenant deviate from the assigned pool.
- DNS failure rate: >1% NXDOMAIN for internal domains over 10m window
- LB health-check flaps: >5% unhealthy over 5m

Outstanding decisions / open questions
- How granular should tenant-based NAT be for small customers to avoid cost explosion? (action: propose tiered model: free-tier shared NAT, enterprise dedicated NAT)
- On-prem: standardized forwarder image and the configuration management approach (Helm chart vs docker+systemd).

Appendix: quick terraform module signature examples (interface only)
- nat module inputs: vpc_id, subnet_map, tenant_map (tenant_id -> egress_pool), tags
- nat module outputs: nat_gateway_ids, nat_ip_pools (map)

-- end playbook (working draft).

Notes to self: follow up with SRE on observability panel changes, schedule dry-run for staging tenant next week, and add a preflight Conftest policy to fail Terraform if any ingress rule uses 0.0.0.0/0 without an exception ticket.
